content: Childhood vaccination is highly effective in preventing pertussis. In the United States, routine childhood vaccination is conducted using the DTaP vaccine, which combines acellular pertussis vaccine with tetanus and diphtheria toxoids. Concerns about the safety of whole-cell pertussis vaccines led to the development of acellular pertussis vaccines. These vaccines are less likely to cause adverse events because they contain purified antigenic components of Bordetella pertussis. Two DTaP vaccines, ACEL-IMUNE® and Tripedia®, were initially licensed for administration of the fourth and fifth doses in children aged 15 months to 6 years who had previously received three or more doses of the whole-cell DTP vaccine. Studies have shown that acellular pertussis vaccines, when administered to infants at 2, 4, and 6 months of age, are effective in preventing pertussis disease and are associated with fewer local, systemic, and serious adverse events compared to whole-cell vaccines. Based on these findings, the FDA has licensed three DTaP vaccines for use in children aged 6 weeks to 6 years. Tripedia® is now licensed for the initial four doses, ACEL-IMUNE® for all five doses, and Infanrix™ for the initial four doses. These vaccines are recommended for routine vaccination of infants and young children, although whole-cell pertussis vaccines remain acceptable alternatives. In September 1996, the FDA licensed the use of TriHIBit™ (ActHIB® reconstituted with Tripedia®) for the fourth dose in the vaccination series against diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis, and Haemophilus influenzae type b disease. This statement provides information on whole-cell pertussis vaccines currently licensed in the United States, summarizes recent studies on the immunogenicity, efficacy, and safety of acellular pertussis vaccines in infants and young children, presents recommendations for the use of Tripedia®, TriHIBit™, ACEL-IMUNE®, and Infanrix™, and supplements previous recommendations on pertussis vaccination. Four DTP vaccines, combining diphtheria and tetanus toxoids with whole-cell pertussis, are currently licensed in the United States. These vaccines, prepared from inactivated Bordetella pertussis bacterial cells, have been used for routine infant vaccination since the mid-1940s. Controlled efficacy trials in the 1940s and subsequent observational studies have shown that a primary series of four doses of whole-cell DTP vaccine is 70%-90% effective in preventing serious pertussis disease. However, adverse events such as drowsiness, irritability, and anorexia are common, while more serious events like seizures (with or without fever) and hypotonic hyporesponsive episodes occur less frequently (approximately 1 case per 1,750 doses). Experts disagree on whether the whole-cell pertussis vaccine causes lasting brain damage, but if it does, such cases are exceedingly rare. Concerns about safety prompted the development of acellular pertussis vaccines, which are associated with fewer adverse events and are effective in preventing pertussis disease. Infection with pertussis induces immunity, but this immunity is not long-lasting, and reinfection is possible. Efforts to develop an inactivated whole-cell pertussis vaccine began after B. pertussis was grown in pure culture in 1906. In 1925, Danish physician Thorvald Madsen tested a whole-cell pertussis vaccine on a large scale to control outbreaks in the Faroe Islands. In 1942, American scientist Pearl Kendrick combined the whole-cell pertussis vaccine with diphtheria and tetanus toxoids to create the first DTP combination vaccine. To reduce the frequent side effects caused by the pertussis component, Japanese scientist Yugi Sato developed an acellular pertussis vaccine in 1981, consisting of filamentous hemagglutinin (FHA) and pertussis toxin (PT), secreted by B. pertussis. Later versions of acellular pertussis vaccines used in other countries included additional defined components of B. pertussis and were often part of the DTaP combination vaccine. Pertussis vaccines are highly effective, strongly recommended, and save many infant lives annually. Although their protection lasts only a few years, they are administered to ensure immunity during childhood, the period of greatest exposure and risk. Immunizations are given in combination with tetanus and diphtheria vaccines at 2, 4, and 6 months of age, with booster doses at 15–18 months, 4–6 years, and 11 years. The short-term effectiveness of the vaccines and the presence of B. pertussis infection in adults and adolescents, who may transmit the bacteria to infants, have led to calls for booster immunizations at later ages. The United States and Germany have approved booster shots for adolescents, adults, or both, while other countries have discontinued pertussis vaccination after age seven due to concerns about side effects associated with the earlier whole-cell vaccines, which tended to increase with age. The whole-cell vaccine is still used in poorer countries due to its lower cost compared to the newer acellular formulations. As immunity from infection or vaccination lasts only a few years, the discontinuation of booster vaccination in older individuals has led to a large pool of susceptible older persons, resulting in an increase in adult-onset pertussis cases since about 2004. This resurgence poses serious public health risks, particularly to newborns who are exposed to pertussis circulating in adolescents or adults before their vaccinations are completed. The decision to resume vaccinating teens and adults reflects the reduced incidence of adverse effects observed with the newer acellular vaccine (DTaP). An acellular vaccine preparation for adults and adolescents has been approved in Canada, Europe, and the United States. The FDA has authorized the use of Boostrix (GlaxoSmithKline) for 10–18-year-olds and Adacel (Sanofi Pasteur) for 11–64-year-olds. These vaccines are recommended for all teens and adults within the indicated age ranges, except for those with a history of adverse reactions to whole-cell pertussis vaccines. The most serious side effects of traditional whole-cell pertussis immunizations were neurological, including seizures and hypotonic episodes. Much of the controversy surrounding the DTP vaccine in the 1970s and 1980s related to whether the whole-cell pertussis component caused permanent brain injury in rare cases. While it was well-established that the pertussis component accounted for most minor local and systemic side effects, several studies failed to show a causal relationship between DTP administration and permanent brain injury. However, criticism of these studies and anecdotal reports of DTP-induced disability and death fueled anti-DTP movements. By the late 1970s, adverse reaction publicity caused immunization rates to fall in several countries, leading to a dramatic increase in pertussis incidence. These developments prompted Yugi Sato to introduce a safer acellular pertussis vaccine in Japan in 1981, though other countries continued using the whole-cell DTP formulation. In the United States, low profit margins and an increase in vaccine-related lawsuits led many manufacturers to stop producing the DTP vaccine by the early 1980s. The 1982 documentary DTP: Vaccine Roulette highlighted the lives of children with severe disabilities allegedly caused by the DTP vaccine, leading to a surge in lawsuits against vaccine manufacturers. By 1985, manufacturers faced difficulty obtaining liability insurance, and the price of the DTP vaccine skyrocketed, causing shortages. To address this crisis, Congress passed the National Childhood Vaccine Injury Act (NCVIA) in 1986, establishing a federal no-fault system to compensate victims of vaccine-related injuries. Since then, vaccine prices have stabilized, and lawsuits against DTP manufacturers have decreased. Most claims filed through the NCVIA have been related to injuries allegedly caused by the whole-cell DTP vaccine. The acellular pertussis vaccine was approved in the United States in 1992 for use in the DTaP combination vaccine. Research has shown the acellular vaccine to be safe, with few reports of adverse effects. Although the whole-cell DTP vaccine is no longer used in the United States, it is still purchased by the World Health Organization and distributed to developing nations due to its lower cost. Close contacts of pertussis cases can be protected from developing symptomatic disease if they receive appropriate antibiotics (chemoprophylaxis) during the 7–21 day incubation period. Close contacts are defined as anyone exposed to the respiratory secretions of an infected person within 21 days before or after the onset of the infected person’s cough. Antibiotics should be administered within three weeks of exposure, especially in high-risk settings, using the same doses as in treatment schedules. Recommended antimicrobial agents for treatment or chemoprophylaxis of pertussis include azithromycin, clarithromycin, and erythromycin. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is also an option. For infants aged ≥1 month, erythromycin, clarithromycin, and azithromycin are preferred for post-exposure prophylaxis. For those aged ≥2 months, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is an alternative to macrolides. For infants <1 month of age, azithromycin is preferred for post-exposure prophylaxis and treatment because it has not been associated with infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis (IHPS), whereas erythromycin has.
